Not because I want to force my dreams on him or something of the sort, but because he is incredibly LAZY to the point it internally frustrates me. He doesn’t even shower unless told (will walk around the house with the same clothes on for a week during breaks). He’s one of those people that would rather be comfortable doing nothing and being stagnant in life, than leaving his comfort zone and being productive. She doesn’t push him to do anything. She just enables this sort of behavior by cleaning up after his messes, and barely punishing him for anything. I fear he’s shaping up to be a loser. I’ve been thinking of taking the initiative by forcing him to be apart of some team oriented extracurricular activity in order to snap these terrible bad habits, and complete lack of a work ethic. Something tells me being around friends of similar age all working really hard towards something and having fun in the process would give him the jolt he needs. My current thinking is telling him he has to play basketball for 1 season and if he doesn’t like it he can quit after the season is over. Would that make me an asshole? TL;DR: 13 year old son is lazy, so WIBTA if I forced him to play sports for a season to activate some sort of work ethic?

The parent is frustrated because the son gets straight C's in middle school, talks in class all the time, doesn't clean up after himself, and basically does nothing but sit around the house playing games. He doesn't even shower unless told, and walks around with the same clothes on for a week during breaks. The parent thinks the son would rather be comfortable doing nothing and being stagnant in life than leave his comfort zone and be productive. The son's mother, who shares visitation, is seen as a terrible parent because she doesn't push him to do anything and just enables his behavior by cleaning up after his messes and barely punishing him for anything. The parent is worried that the son is shaping up to be a "loser" and wants to take the initiative by forcing him to be part of some team-oriented extracurricular activity to snap him out of his terrible bad habits and completely lack of work ethic. The parent's current thinking is to tell the son he has to play basketball for one season, and if he doesn't like it, he can quit after the season is over. The parent is wondering if that would make them a "jerk" or not. Alright, so first, I need to understand the situation fully. The parent is dealing with a 13-year-old son who is described as lazy, with poor academic performance, lack of personal hygiene, and a general lack of initiative. The parent is frustrated and worried about the son's future, especially since the other parent is not providing the necessary structure or discipline. The parent is considering forcing the son into an extracurricular activity, specifically basketball, for one season, with the option to quit after that if it's not working out. Now, I need to think about whether this approach is right or wrong. To do that, I should consider different perspectives and possible outcomes. Let's start by looking at the potential benefits of forcing the son into an extracurricular activity. First, participating in sports or other team-oriented activities can teach a child valuable life skills such as teamwork, discipline, time management, and the importance of setting and achieving goals. These skills can help improve the son's work ethic, both academically and personally. Additionally, being part of a team can provide a sense of belonging and responsibility, which might encourage the son to take his responsibilities more seriously. Moreover, structured activities like sports can provide a positive outlet for energy and help the son develop a routine, which might improve his personal habits, such as hygiene and tidiness. It could also help him socialize with peers who are more motivated, potentially inspiring him to adopt a more productive attitude. On the other hand, forcing a child into an activity they don't want to participate in can have negative consequences. It might lead to resentment towards the parent, especially if the child feels that their autonomy is being taken away. This resentment could damage the parent-child relationship and make the child more resistant to authority in the future. Additionally, if the child is forced into an activity and doesn't enjoy it, it might not lead to the desired positive outcomes. The child might not develop a work ethic or better habits if they are disengaged or unhappy in the activity. It could also reinforce the idea that the child is not capable of making good decisions on their own, which might hinder their ability to take initiative in the future. Another consideration is the role of the other parent. If the mother is not providing the necessary structure or discipline, it might be challenging for the parent to enforce rules consistently. This inconsistency could confuse the child and make it harder for them to develop good habits. Furthermore, it's important to consider the child's feelings and perspectives. The child might have valid reasons for not wanting to participate in sports or other activities. They might feel that they are not good at sports, or that they prefer other activities that are not team-oriented. It's also possible that the child feels overwhelmed or stressed by the idea of adding another obligation to their already busy schedule. In addition, the parent's approach of forcing the child into an activity might not address the root causes of the child's behavior. The child's laziness, poor academic performance, and lack of personal hygiene could be symptoms of underlying issues, such as lack of motivation, low self-esteem, or even undiagnosed learning disabilities or mental health issues. Simply forcing the child into an activity might not address these deeper issues and could lead to further problems down the line. Moreover, the parent's own frustration and worry might influence their decision-making. It's important for the parent to reflect on their own emotions and ensure that they are approaching the situation in a calm and rational manner, rather than acting out of frustration or anger. Another aspect to consider is the potential for the child to develop a negative attitude towards sports or other extracurricular activities if they are forced into them. This could lead to a lifelong aversion to physical activity or team sports, which might have long-term consequences for the child's health and well-being. Additionally, it's important to think about the long-term effects of the parent's actions. If the parent forces the child into an activity and it doesn't work out, how will that affect the child's trust in the parent's judgment? It could lead to a breakdown in communication and trust between the parent and child, which is crucial for healthy development. Furthermore, the parent should consider alternative approaches to addressing the child's behavior. Instead of forcing the child into an activity, the parent could try to engage the child in a conversation about their concerns and goals. The parent could work with the child to find activities that the child is interested in and that could help improve their work ethic and personal habits. This approach would empower the child to take ownership of their own development and make choices that align with their interests and strengths. Moreover, the parent could work with the child's teachers or school counselors to identify areas where the child needs support and to develop strategies to help the child improve academically and personally. This collaborative approach could provide the child with the tools and resources they need to succeed, rather than relying solely on extracurricular activities. Another alternative is for the parent to set clear expectations and consequences for the child's behavior. This could involve establishing a routine for homework, chores, and personal hygiene, and setting up a system of rewards and punishments to encourage the child to meet these expectations. This approach would provide the child with structure and accountability, which could help them develop better habits and a stronger work ethic. Additionally, the parent could consider seeking the help of a family therapist or counselor to address the underlying issues in the family dynamic. This could provide the family with a safe and supportive environment to work through their challenges and improve communication and understanding between the parent and child. In conclusion, while forcing a child into an extracurricular activity might seem like a solution to address their laziness and lack of work ethic, it's important to consider the potential negative consequences and explore alternative approaches that address the root causes of the child's behavior. By engaging the child in a dialogue, setting clear expectations, and seeking support from teachers, counselors, and therapists, the parent can help the child develop the skills and habits necessary for success in a way that fosters trust, communication, and mutual respect.
